name: David Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What does a usual site day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead carpentry on house extensions and loft conversions, fitting beams, stairs and doors into rooms that were not built square. I have a trade certificate and years of experience making an old wall agree with a new plan. The puzzle is what I enjoy.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day to make cutting lists and show clients kitchen layouts, then I measure the real space. Hannah, my partner, works at a farm supply shop; we have two school-age children, a mortgage and more than six months saved. I also rent a mini-digger and van on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our extension crew the AI kitchen pictures still help clients choose a layout, even if the bigger claims fizzle. A drawing on a tablet never cuts a beam square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah and I have the mortgage under control, more than six months saved and two wages. I earn well as the lead carpenter, with plenty of builders nearby, so a plateau leaves us in a sound place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting loft stairs and using my existing daily design app for client meetings. I would keep renting out the mini-digger and spare van on weekends, but wait for six paid hire bookings before buying another machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I might wish the app did more, but the children’s bills and our work remain steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would six bookings prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough paid demand to cover the deposit and insurance on another digger. An enquiry from a neighbour does not count until money comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your wife need to work more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Hannah’s hours at the farm supply shop cover their share now, and neither of us needs to chase extra shifts for this picture.

say: I would keep using **AI kitchen sketches** to discuss extensions with clients.
I would tell the crew that **beam fitting** still needs measurements on the actual house.
think: Our **two wages** and strong savings make the mortgage secure in this world.
My **hire equipment** is useful extra income, though demand must be paid before expansion.
do: Keep **loft carpentry** and existing daily design app use.
Keep renting the **mini-digger and van** without buying a second machine yet.
feel: **Calm** about work and the family budget.
S0.quote: An enquiry from a neighbour does not count until money comes in.
fieldNote: He has a strong cushion, high pay and **many local builders**, making the plateau comfortable.
The equipment hire is already **existing income**; a second digger remains conditional on paid demand.

steps.text: Keep loft carpentry and existing design app and equipment hire work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can book timber and draw kitchens faster, but the client still needs a builder who knows the old walls. I would want a trial before software starts ordering steel for our extensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office might use fewer planners, while I still have hands-on work. My own hours look secure, yet Hannah’s shop could see customers change jobs and spend less on farm supplies; I would watch that second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI steel-ordering controls if the builder lets me test them on one extension. I would compare the order with the engineer’s signed plan and refuse a delivery that does not match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the shop and the office, not afraid for my next pay packet. We have savings if demand softens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change household spending today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Hannah’s shop has not lost sales yet, and we would use actual monthly figures before changing family plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a trial convincing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software must match the signed beam size and delivery date on a real extension. I would not put a wall opening on a guess.

say: I would insist on a **real-extension trial** before AI orders steel.
I would keep an **engineer-signed plan** beside each beam delivery.
think: My **carpentry hours** look safe while office planning changes.
Hannah’s **shop income** could weaken if customers spend less, though we have a buffer.
do: Learn new **AI steel-order controls** through a one-extension trial if the builder grants access.
Check the **steel delivery** against the engineer’s signed plan before accepting it.
feel: **Anxious** about possible household income loss through Hannah’s shop.
S1.quote: I would not put a wall opening on a guess.
fieldNote: The second household wage creates a plausible **income risk** even while carpentry stays busy.
New ordering controls are distinct from his **existing design app**, and access depends on the builder.

steps.text: Learn AI steel ordering with builder access on one real extension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell clients thinking AI in 2028 can draw any kitchen, but nobody has a capable robot altering their old house until around 2031. I want trial photos from an actual crooked loft, not a showroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose some extension work after 2031, though my equipment hire, savings and nearby contractors provide alternatives. The mortgage and two school-age children still need regular income, so I cannot call the change harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid carpentry shifts and ask the builder about a posted robot-site supervisor vacancy. If a role with funded training on paid time and a firm wage covering the mortgage opens, I would train and apply; otherwise I would search posted local carpentry jobs only after two reduced rosters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, with options to act. I would not gamble the family’s safe cushion on a machine job that has not been offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for any supervisor title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I need the written hours and wage, including what happens between projects. A title without paid weeks would be worse than my current carpentry job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the mini-digger hire replace lost wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It helps with extras, but weekend bookings are not a full weekday wage. I would count only paid hires, not enquiries.

I would ask for **crooked-loft trials** before a builder cuts human carpenters.
think: My **extension hours** could shrink when robots reach hands-on work.
Savings and nearby work help, but **hire income** cannot replace a full wage.
do: Keep **paid extension shifts** while builder work continues.
Train for a **posted paid supervisor role** only with funded study time and mortgage-covering wages.
Search **posted local carpentry jobs** after two reduced rosters if no suitable role appears.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible hours loss, while still able to choose among options.
S2.quote: A title without paid weeks would be worse than my current carpentry job.
fieldNote: He keeps **funding and wages** with paid time attached to the possible supervisor role.
The local search follows **two reduced rosters**, and hire bookings are not treated as guaranteed replacement pay.

steps.text: Keep paid extension shifts while builder work continues
Train only for posted paid supervisor role with funded time and mortgage-covering wage
Search posted local carpentry jobs after two reduced rosters if no suitable role appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to test a robot cutting in an old roof without putting a family downstairs at risk. I would join a paid trial if the builder posts a place for experienced carpenters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 may make drawings cheap; hands-on robots come around 2034. I will be fifty one then, with years of mortgage and school costs left, but the longer run lets me learn a proven site control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep building extensions next year and ask for a paid two-week robot-safety trial when the company advertises one. If selected, I would learn the controls, log failed stops and apply only for a posted role with enough paid weeks to cover our household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with an appetite to test the real thing. A careful two-week trial tells me more than a hundred glossy pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you start a safe trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the saw isolated and the power off while we mark the exclusion area. A qualified operator can restart it for a supervised cut after everyone is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use your savings to fund those two weeks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A company trial should pay wages, not send the bill home to my children. I will not fund a manufacturer’s demonstration from our savings.

say: I would require **old-roof trials** before 2034 carpentry robots work over occupied rooms.
I would begin with **isolated saws** and a supervised restart.
think: I still need **paid work** at fifty one, even with strong savings.
Five years may bring a **proven control role** if the builder posts one.
do: Join a **paid two-week trial** if posted and learn controls before applying for mortgage-covering work.
feel: **Uneasy** about future job shape, willing to test a safe paid machine.
S3.quote: A company trial should pay wages, not send the bill home to my children.
fieldNote: He would learn controls through **paid company work**, not buy a speculative certificate.
The trial starts with **power off** and an exclusion area, then supervised cutting.

steps.text: Keep paid extension carpentry shifts while requesting advertised paid trial place
Join advertised paid two-week robot trial if selected and learn controls
Mark exclusion area with saw isolated and power off before supervised restart when clear
Apply only to posted control role with paid weeks covering household costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices ten years is time to learn a trade and become useful before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. I would still teach them to measure an old wall twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty six when robots reach hands-on work and likely still need my main wage. Our savings and equipment assets give choices. An occasional digger hire is not a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep building extensions and hiring the digger in 2026. I would add fifty from each regular wage to savings if Hannah’s shop hours and the mortgage remain covered; in the first year after 2036 I would inspect actual site vacancies before changing work, and after 2039 I would apply only to a posted role with comparable paid weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about long-run work, comfortable about next month. I would rather build the reserve from a real wage than count on imaginary machine demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy another digger this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if six paid hire bookings cover the deposit, insurance and storage. Otherwise the current equipment is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early to avoid robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I will still have household costs in my fifties. The plan is to keep earning, even if the tools change.

say: I would protect **apprentice practice** before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 robots alter building work.
I would keep **old-wall measurements** in the trade lessons.
think: I expect to need **carpentry wages** around 2039.
Our **assets and savings** provide options but hire income remains uneven.
do: Keep **2026 extension work** and hire bookings while customers pay.
Save **fifty extra monthly** from wages only if Hannah’s hours and mortgage costs allow.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant job change while current income is secure.
S4.quote: An occasional digger hire is not a salary.
fieldNote: The extra transfer is genuine **new wage saving**, conditional on shop hours and housing costs.
The later search still requires a **posted comparable-pay role**, with 2026 work stated separately.

steps.text: Keep paid extension carpentry and existing digger hire during 2026
Save fifty extra monthly from wages only if shop hours and mortgage costs allow
Inspect actual site vacancies after 2036 before changing work
Apply after 2039 only for posted construction role offering comparable paid weeks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could reduce extension work around 2031 while the mortgage and children still need a full wage. Paid training for a posted site role and real old-house trials would help me act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a machine can tell a client a beam size is wrong before the roof is opened. A nice picture cannot hold up a bedroom.

headlineQuote: A nice picture cannot hold up a bedroom.
portrait: **David**, 43, leads extension carpentry with a trade certificate, high pay, strong savings and many nearby builders.
He uses **AI daily** for plans and client designs and earns extra from already-owned hire equipment.
Hannah’s **shop wage**, their mortgage and two school-age children make stable paid weeks more important than a new job title.
The **2028 case** worries him because robots could reach hands-on extension work in 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce his paid extension weeks around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training for a **posted site role** and real old-house trials would help.
